lead: Reinforcement is supplied in fixed lengths, so bars must be joined; a lap splice overlaps two bars so force passes from one to the other through bond. Curtailment stops bars where bending moment has fallen, saving steel, but only after development length is satisfied. Both ideas protect the same thing: every bar force must have a safe path into concrete. They appear in beam schedules, bar bending schedules and site checks. Only a few universities teach this as a separate chapter.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.5 for Ld and Unit 2 for the bending moment envelope.

blocks.text: What a lap is. A lap splice overlaps two bars over a length Llap. Force leaves the ending bar through bond into concrete and enters the continuing bar over the same overlap. A 16 m beam cannot use one 12 m stock bar, so a joint is needed. The lap needs concrete around both bars and ties to hold them. Some syllabi call this splicing of reinforcement. A lap joins bars within a span; it does not replace end anchorage at a support.

blocks.where: Llap is the overlap length in mm; Ld is the development length from Chapter 3.5 in mm; φ is the bar diameter in mm. 30φ is the flexural tension minimum.

blocks.text: In flexural tension, L<sub>lap</sub> is the larger of L<sub>d</sub> and 30φ. In compression the demand is lower: a compression lap is at least max(compression L<sub>d</sub>, 24φ). When diameters differ, use the larger bar diameter, which gives the greater development length.
Stagger adjacent laps. If all laps fall at one section, that section has many interrupted bars. Keep clear spacing and do not crowd a lap with other steel.

Theoretical cut-off. Bending moment falls from midspan toward a support. Extra bars can stop where the remaining bars alone carry the design moment. Find that point from the bending moment envelope, which covers all load arrangements. It is the theoretical cut-off.

Shift by max(Ld, 12φ). At the theoretical cut-off the bar still carries force. That force needs bond length. Move the actual cut-off by at least max(Ld, 12φ) toward the low-moment end, so the bar continues that length beyond the theoretical point. A cut exactly at zero moment is wrong: zero moment does not mean zero bar force.

Cut in steps. Curtail one pair, check the remaining section, then the next. Each step changes steel area, anchorage and shear. Provide stirrups near a cut-off because the tensile force changes abruptly. The figure shows a 6 m beam with two full-length bars and two bars from 1.5 m to 4.5 m. Detail the final shape as in Chapter 3.7.

figure.caption: The shorter pair is curtailed from 1.5 m to 4.5 m in the 6 m beam, leaving a 3 m central length. Each end must continue at least max(L<sub>d</sub>, 12φ) beyond the theoretical cut-off.

spec.aria: Two bottom bars run full length; two are curtailed from 1.5 m to 4.5 m in a 6 m beam.

examples.question: A 6 m simply supported beam has four 16 mm bars at midspan. Two bars are curtailed 1.5 m from each support, leaving a 3 m central length. For a 16 mm bar, L<sub>d</sub> = 1.03 m. Check a 1.2 m lap when the flexural tension minimum is 30φ. State the extension beyond the theoretical cut-off.
steps: φ = 16 mm. Minimum lap = 30φ = 30 × 16 = 480 mm = 0.48 m.
Provided lap = 1.2 m = 1200 mm. 1200 > 1030, so the lap is adequate; spare = 170 mm = 0.17 m.

At a cut-off the extension is max(L<sub>d</sub>, 12φ) = max(1030, 12 × 16) = max(1030, 192) = 1030 mm = 1.03 m. With the actual end at 1.5 m from the support, the theoretical point can be at 1.5 + 1.03 = 2.53 m from the support.
examples.answer: The 1.2 m lap is adequate (required 1.03 m), and each curtailed bar needs max(L<sub>d</sub>, 12φ) = 1.03 m of extension beyond its theoretical cut-off.
examples.check:
phi_mm = 16
min_lap_mm = 30 * phi_mm
Ld_m = 1.03
req_lap_m = max(Ld_m, min_lap_mm / 1000)
provided_m = 1.2
spare_m = provided_m - req_lap_m
extension_m = max(Ld_m, 12 * phi_mm / 1000)
theoretical_m = 1.5 + extension_m
print(min_lap_mm / 1000)
print(Ld_m)
print(req_lap_m)
print(provided_m)
print(round(spare_m, 3))
print(theoretical_m)

traps: Cutting a bar at the theoretical point of zero moment instead of shifting the cut-off by L<sub>d</sub>.
Using a lap shorter than L<sub>d</sub>, or forgetting the 30φ minimum in flexural tension.
Placing all laps at one section instead of staggering them.
Treating a compression lap with the tension minimum, or using the smaller bar diameter when bars differ.

quiz.a: An overlap of two bars that transfers force by bond from one bar to the other.

quiz.q: Why must a curtailed bar extend beyond the theoretical cut-off?
quiz.a: The bar carries force at that point; the extension provides at least max(L<sub>d</sub>, 12φ) so bond can anchor the force.

quiz.q: A 20 mm bar has L<sub>d</sub> = 1.4 m. Find the minimum flexural tension lap.
Why stagger laps along a beam?
quiz.a: To avoid one weak section with many interrupted bars; it spreads force transfer and reduces congestion.

quiz.q: Actual cut-off is 1.2 m from a support; L<sub>d</sub> = 0.9 m. Where can the theoretical cut-off lie?
quiz.a: At least 1.2 + 0.9 = 2.1 m from the support when L<sub>d</sub> governs; add 12φ instead if it is greater than L<sub>d</sub>.

quiz.q: State the flexural tension lap rule in symbols.

beyond: Not for the exam. Site practice uses bar bending schedules and mechanical couplers where laps would be too congested. Couplers transfer force by threads or sleeves, not bond. Seismic detailing restricts lap locations in plastic hinge zones. Search next for mechanical splices for reinforcement and bar bending schedule.
